title: Least privilege and output controls
summary: Give each identity and tool the minimum it needs, treat model output as untrusted, and put a human in front of actions that are costly or irreversible. Limits on what an attack can do matter more than perfect detection.
useIf: Your assistant calls tools, writes to systems or runs with a service identity.
avoidIf: You are choosing the document ACL mechanism. Least privilege sits around it and does not replace it.

explain.md: OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency lists four mitigations: **minimise the extensions** the model can call, **minimise each extension's functions**, **avoid open-ended extensions** such as run-a-shell-command or fetch-a-URL, and **minimise the permissions** the extension holds, enforced through the identity it uses. Its example: an agent that recommends products needs read access to a products table, with no access to other tables and no insert, update or delete [[tr5]].

explain.caption: One identity per job
head: Identity
Holds
Does not hold
rows: The caller's delegated token. In Azure AI Search the calling app needs Search Index Data Reader [[r12]]
Read on sources and write on the index. SharePoint indexing needs application permissions [[r16]]
Any role used at query time
The minimum rights for one task, per user where possible
A dedicated role for elevated read, which sees all documents [[r12]]

explain.md: **Output controls** apply OWASP LLM05: encode, validate and apply a content security policy (see the exfiltration topic) [[tr4]]. Add citation hygiene: show titles and links only for documents the caller may open, since a title can leak. Scan for secrets and personal data where leaks are text patterns.

**Human review** belongs on actions that are irreversible, externally visible or sensitive. Microsoft Agent Framework has a built-in hook: in Python a `@tool` with `approval_mode="always_require"`, with `user_input_requests` on the run result, and in .NET `ApprovalRequiredAIFunction`, which produces `ToolApprovalRequestContent` [[tr17]]. When untrusted input, private data and an external action all appear, require approval or remove a leg [[r10]].

explain.title: Review is a control only if it works
explain.md: Show the reviewer the evidence (sources, the filter used, the exact action), not only a yes or no button. A queue that reviewers approve in bulk adds delay and no safety.

pitfalls.fix: Use a read-only role limited to the needed tables and enforce it in the database

scenarios.title: One admin key in the application
scenarios.situation: A small team ships an assistant that uses the search service's admin key for queries, ingestion and debugging because it was quick. The assistant serves 300 employees.
constraints: Per-user permissions exist in the index
unknowns: Does the app pass the user's token to the search service?
scenarios.question: What do you change first?

options.name: Leave it and add a prompt rule about confidential documents
options.why: A prompt is not enforcement and the key reaches everything.
options.tradeoff: A tone rule helps only alongside real controls.

options.name: Split identities: query-time with the user's token and Search Index Data Reader, a separate ingestion identity, and a dedicated elevated-read role for debugging
options.why: Each identity holds only what its job needs, and ACL filters apply at query time [[r12]].

options.name: Rotate the admin key monthly
options.tradeoff: The key still holds every right, so a leak is still total.

flips.then: A single read-only identity is enough.
Build the filter server side and still split ingestion from query.

scenarios.title: A run-any-SQL tool
scenarios.situation: An analytics assistant has a tool that runs SQL the model writes, using a credential that can read and write several schemas. Documents in the knowledge base are user-authored.
unknowns: Which tables does the task need?
scenarios.question: How do you reduce the risk?

options.name: Add a system prompt rule: never run destructive statements
options.why: Injected text can override the rule, and the credential still allows damage.

options.name: Replace it with narrow, parameterised functions and a read-only database role limited to the needed tables
options.why: It applies minimise-functions and minimise-permissions from LLM06 and enforces them in the database [[tr5]].
options.tradeoff: Less flexibility for new questions, so add functions as needs appear.

options.name: Keep run-any-SQL but require approval for each statement
options.tradeoff: Reviewer fatigue and the credential stays broad.

flips.if: Only analysts use it in a sandbox copy
flips.then: Open-ended SQL on a read-only replica may be acceptable.

flips.if: Queries are always one of ten shapes

scenarios.takeaway: Replace open-ended tools with narrow ones.

scenarios.title: Four thousand drafts a day
scenarios.situation: An agent drafts customer replies, about 4,000 a day. Replies can contain account data. A reviewer team currently approves every draft and has started approving in bulk.
unknowns: Which replies are irreversible or sensitive?
scenarios.question: How do you redesign review?

options.name: Approve every draft with a simple yes or no
options.why: At this volume reviewers stop checking, so it adds delay and no safety.
options.tradeoff: Right for a small number of high-stakes actions.

options.name: Risk-tier: approval with evidence for replies that carry account data or external links, templated auto-send for low-risk replies and a sampled audit
options.why: Reviewer attention goes where harm is possible, and the audit measures the rest.
options.tradeoff: A tiering rule to maintain and some late detection on sampled items.

options.name: Remove human review and add an output filter
options.tradeoff: Filters miss paraphrased or encoded data and nothing gates the action.

flips.if: Volume falls to a few dozen per day
flips.then: Approve all with evidence on screen.

flips.if: A regulator requires oversight for the class of decision
flips.then: Design review to meet that duty, with an audit trail.

scenarios.takeaway: Tier human review by risk and show evidence.

quiz.q: Which role should the application hold for query-time calls to Azure AI Search with native ACLs, following least privilege?
options: Search Index Data Contributor, so it can fix data
Search Service Contributor, so it can manage indexes
Search Index Data Reader, with the user's token in the header
quiz.explain: The caller needs Search Index Data Reader (or Contributor) and the user's token for ACL matching. Reader is the least privilege. Contributor, service contributor and owner grant write or management rights the query path never needs.

quiz.q: Which are OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency mitigations? Choose all that apply.
options: Minimise the extensions an agent can call
Avoid open-ended extensions such as running any shell command
Give the agent a broad admin credential so it never fails
Minimise the permissions extensions hold in other systems
quiz.explain: OWASP lists minimising extensions, their functions and their permissions, and avoiding open-ended extensions. A broad credential is the opposite of least privilege.

flashcards.front: What are the four LLM06 mitigations?
flashcards.back: Minimise extensions, minimise their functions, avoid open-ended extensions (shell, fetch URL) and minimise their permissions, enforced through the identity they use.

flashcards.front: Which identities should be separate in a RAG system?
flashcards.back: Query-time retrieval (the user's token), ingestion (source read, index write), tool execution (task-specific) and admin debugging (dedicated elevated-read role).

flashcards.front: How does Agent Framework gate a tool call for approval?
flashcards.back: Python: @tool with approval_mode always_require, with user_input_requests on the result. .NET: wrap in ApprovalRequiredAIFunction, which yields ToolApprovalRequestContent.
